May improve parkinsonian symptoms and drug-induced extrapyramidal reactions.

statements.text: Treatment of idiopathic Parkinson disease, postencephalitic parkinsonism, symptomatic parkinsonism, and drug-induced extrapyramidal reactions as described in the label.

Adverse effects span CNS/psychiatric, cardiovascular/edema, ocular, gastrointestinal, dermatologic, and anticholinergic-like domains.
Contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to amantadine or product components.
Dose reduction is required in renal impairment and often in older adults because accumulation can cause severe toxicity.
Use caution in patients with seizure disorders, psychiatric illness, heart failure/edema, or untreated angle-closure glaucoma; monitor for visual changes and corneal edema.
Do not stop abruptly in patients treated for Parkinson disease because abrupt withdrawal can worsen symptoms or precipitate an NMS-like syndrome.
Mean elimination half-life in healthy adults is approximately 17 ± 4 hours and becomes markedly prolonged with renal impairment.
Amantadine is eliminated predominantly unchanged in urine; hemodialysis removes negligible amounts.
After oral administration, peak plasma concentrations generally occur about 2–4 hours after a dose.
Concomitant anticholinergic drugs may increase anticholinergic-like adverse effects; CNS stimulants may increase CNS stimulation.
Quinine or quinidine can reduce renal clearance and increase amantadine concentrations.
The label gives timing precautions with live attenuated influenza vaccine because antiviral therapy may interfere with vaccine virus replication.
Monitor renal function and adjust the dose accordingly; assess mental status, suicidality/psychosis, edema/heart failure, seizures, vision/corneal symptoms, and impulse-control behavior.
Pregnancy data are limited and the label describes potential fetal risk; use requires an individualized benefit–risk assessment.
Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment in the cited label.
Substantial dose reduction is required; half-life can extend to days in severe impairment and dialysis does not effectively remove the drug.
Safety and effectiveness for influenza indications are not established below 1 year of age in the cited label.
Older adults commonly require lower doses because renal clearance declines with age.

Overdose can be fatal and may produce severe CNS, cardiac, renal, respiratory, and anticholinergic-like toxicity; management is supportive with close ECG, electrolyte, renal, and neurologic monitoring.

Renal elimination, poor dialyzability, hallucinations, edema, and livedo reticularis are important toxicity clues.

statements.text: Blocks potassium, sodium, and calcium currents and exerts noncompetitive antisympathetic effects, thereby prolonging action-potential duration and refractoriness while slowing conduction.
Its dominant class III effect prolongs repolarization and refractoriness, while additional sodium-channel, calcium-channel, and beta-adrenergic effects contribute to AV nodal and conduction slowing.
Suppresses recurrent ventricular fibrillation and hemodynamically unstable ventricular tachycardia but can also cause bradycardia, conduction block, QT prolongation, and proarrhythmia.

Oral tablets are indicated only for documented recurrent ventricular fibrillation and recurrent hemodynamically unstable ventricular tachycardia when other available antiarrhythmics have failed or are not tolerated.
Commonly encountered reactions include corneal microdeposits, gastrointestinal symptoms, bradycardia, photosensitivity, and thyroid dysfunction.

Serious toxicities include potentially fatal pulmonary toxicity, hepatic injury, worsening arrhythmia, severe bradycardia/heart block, thyroid hypo- or hyperfunction, optic neuropathy/neuritis, and fetal toxicity.
Blue-gray skin discoloration and peripheral neuropathy are clinically important long-term adverse effects.
Toxicity is multisystem: pulmonary, hepatic, cardiac, thyroid, ocular, neurologic, dermatologic, and reproductive.

Boxed warning: amiodarone has potentially fatal pulmonary, hepatic, and cardiac toxicity and should be reserved for the labeled life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias; initiation requires specialist supervision and appropriate monitoring.

Contraindicated in cardiogenic shock; marked sinus-node dysfunction or second-/third-degree AV block causing bradycardia or syncope without a functioning pacemaker; and hypersensitivity to the drug or components.
Correct hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypocalcemia before treatment because electrolyte disturbances increase proarrhythmic risk.

Pulmonary symptoms, hepatic injury, visual changes, thyroid dysfunction, bradycardia, neuropathy, photosensitivity, and interactions can emerge during therapy or after discontinuation because of the long half-life.
Therapeutic onset after oral loading is delayed and variable because of extensive distribution and slow accumulation.
Pharmacologic effects and adverse reactions can persist for weeks to months after discontinuation.
After chronic oral therapy, mean terminal half-life is about 58 days for amiodarone and 36 days for its active metabolite desethylamiodarone, with very wide ranges.
Metabolized primarily by CYP3A and CYP2C8 to desethylamiodarone and is a clinically important inhibitor of multiple CYP enzymes and P-glycoprotein.
Elimination is primarily hepatic/biliary; urinary excretion is negligible and the drug is not dialyzable.
Amiodarone increases exposure to warfarin, digoxin, several statins, and other CYP/P-glycoprotein substrates; dose reduction and close monitoring are often required.
Avoid or carefully manage other QT-prolonging drugs and negative chronotropes because of torsades, bradycardia, and conduction-block risk.

Before and during therapy, monitor ECG/rhythm and electrolytes, liver tests, thyroid function, chest imaging and pulmonary status; obtain ophthalmic evaluation for visual symptoms and review all interacting drugs.
Can cause fetal harm, including neonatal thyroid and cardiac effects; use requires a compelling benefit–risk justification.
Breastfeeding is not recommended because amiodarone and its metabolite are present in human milk and contain substantial iodine.
Renal elimination is negligible, but renal impairment does not remove the need for intensive toxicity and interaction monitoring.
Hepatic injury can be severe or fatal; baseline and periodic liver testing is required and dose reduction or discontinuation may be necessary.
Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients are not established in the cited oral label.
Older adults may be more susceptible to bradycardia and organ toxicity; dosing should be individualized with close monitoring.
Overdose may cause hypotension, bradycardia, AV block, ventricular arrhythmias, and hepatic injury; treatment is supportive, and dialysis is ineffective.
The cited oral label is much narrower than the common teaching shorthand “AF/VT”: it approves only specified recurrent life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias.
Very long half-life plus pulmonary, hepatic, thyroid, ocular, and cardiac toxicity makes baseline and longitudinal monitoring central.

Treatment of susceptible infections of the ear/nose/throat, genitourinary tract, skin/skin structures, and lower respiratory tract as specified in the label.
As part of labeled combination regimens with acid suppression and other antibiotics for H. pylori infection associated with duodenal ulcer disease.

Drug-induced enterocolitis syndrome (DIES), a non-IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction, is a rare but clinically important labeled risk.
Adverse effects primarily involve gastrointestinal, allergic/dermatologic, hepatic, hematologic, renal, and neurologic systems.
Contraindicated in patients with a history of a serious hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin or other beta-lactam antibacterials.
Evaluate prior beta-lactam allergy and discontinue promptly if an allergic reaction occurs.
Use only for proven or strongly suspected susceptible bacterial infection to reduce resistance; assess severe or persistent diarrhea for C. difficile.
Rash is common in infectious mononucleosis; avoid empiric use for that syndrome unless bacterial infection is established.
The elimination half-life is short in patients with normal renal function and becomes prolonged as renal function declines.
Eliminated predominantly by the kidneys; probenecid reduces renal tubular secretion and increases/prolongs concentrations.
Oral amoxicillin is acid-stable and is absorbed after oral administration; food does not preclude use of the cited oral formulations.

Allopurinol coadministration is associated with a higher frequency of rash; oral anticoagulant effects may be altered and require monitoring.
Monitor clinical response, allergy/rash, severe diarrhea, and renal function; with prolonged therapy, periodically assess hematologic, renal, and hepatic function.
Available human experience has not established a drug-associated major-birth-defect risk, but use should remain indication-driven.
Amoxicillin is present in human milk; monitor the breastfed infant for sensitization, diarrhea, or candidiasis.
Dose or interval adjustment is required in severe renal impairment; some high-strength tablets are unsuitable below specified glomerular-filtration thresholds.
Oral formulations are labeled for pediatric use with age/weight-specific dosing; neonatal renal immaturity requires careful dosing.
Because renal elimination is important, dose selection in older adults should account for kidney function.
Overdose may cause gastrointestinal symptoms, crystalluria, renal injury, or seizures; provide supportive care, maintain hydration, and consider hemodialysis in severe cases.
Aminopenicillin: beta-lactam/PBP-mediated cell-wall inhibition; beta-lactamase can inactivate the drug unless an appropriate inhibitor-containing regimen is used.
H. pylori is a combination-regimen indication, not evidence that amoxicillin monotherapy is an eradication regimen.

statements.text: Competitively inhibits acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors in peripheral organs and, at sufficient exposure, the central nervous system.

Reduces salivary and respiratory secretions, opposes vagally mediated bradycardia, dilates pupils, reduces gastrointestinal and urinary smooth-muscle tone, and can produce dose-dependent central excitation or delirium.
Reverses life-threatening muscarinic manifestations of organophosphorus or muscarinic-mushroom poisoning; it does not reactivate inhibited acetylcholinesterase.
Provides temporary vagolytic treatment for clinically significant bradycardia and reduces secretions in appropriate peri-procedural settings.
Temporary blockade of severe or life-threatening muscarinic effects, including antidotal use in organophosphorus and muscarinic-mushroom poisoning.

The selected U.S. injection label includes antisialagogue/antivagal use and bradyasystolic-cardiac-arrest dosing; the 2025 AHA guideline separately supports atropine for acute bradycardia with hemodynamic compromise, so the website must distinguish bradycardia with a pulse from nonshockable cardiac arrest.

statements.text: Expected antimuscarinic effects include dry mouth, blurred vision/mydriasis, tachycardia, constipation, and urinary hesitancy or retention.
Severe toxicity can cause hyperthermia, ileus, urinary retention, acute angle-closure glaucoma, marked tachyarrhythmia, agitation, delirium, hallucinations, seizures, coma, and respiratory failure.
Paradoxical bradycardia can occur with small doses, and hypersensitivity reactions are possible.
Toxicity reflects muscarinic blockade across ocular, cardiac, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, thermoregulatory, and CNS systems.
The cited emergency-use injection label lists no formal contraindications; this does not remove the need to assess clinical risks such as glaucoma, obstruction, tachyarrhythmia, and ischemia.

Muscarinic blockade can worsen acute glaucoma, pyloric or intestinal obstruction, urinary retention, and respiratory secretion thickening.
Intravenous administration provides rapid antimuscarinic effects suitable for emergency treatment.
Atropine undergoes enzymatic hydrolysis, particularly in the liver; listed metabolites include noratropine, atropine N-oxide, tropine, and tropic acid.
The label reports that approximately 13% to 50% of atropine is excreted unchanged in urine.

After injection, atropine disappears rapidly from the blood and distributes throughout the body; plasma-protein binding is about 44% and is saturable over the concentration range described in the label.
Atropine delays the rate of mexiletine absorption without changing relative oral bioavailability.

During intravenous use, titrate to heart rate, PR interval, blood pressure, and symptoms; in coronary artery disease, keep within the label's lower total-dose limit to reduce tachycardia-related myocardial oxygen demand.
Use in pregnancy requires balancing the maternal emergency indication against limited fetal safety data.
Human-milk data are limited; consider the clinical need and potential anticholinergic effects in the infant.
Pediatric dosing is weight-based and must avoid dosing errors; infants and young children may be particularly susceptible to hyperthermia and CNS toxicity.
Older adults may be more susceptible to delirium, glaucoma, urinary retention, constipation, and tachyarrhythmia.

Antimuscarinic poisoning is managed with airway/ventilatory and cardiovascular support, cooling, seizure control, and specialist toxicology guidance; physostigmine use requires careful case selection and monitoring.
Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist and an organophosphate antidote for muscarinic manifestations; oximes address acetylcholinesterase reactivation and are a separate concept.

Assess QT risk, electrolyte abnormalities, bradyarrhythmia, and concomitant QT-prolonging/CYP3A-interacting drugs before treatment.
Stop and evaluate for hepatic injury or severe diarrhea; use antibacterial stewardship and confirm organism susceptibility when appropriate.
Erythromycin is hepatically handled and is a clinically important inhibitor/substrate in CYP3A-mediated interactions.

The delayed-release formulation protects acid-labile erythromycin until intestinal release; absorption can vary by formulation and food conditions.

Monitor clinical response, gastrointestinal tolerance, liver tests when risk or symptoms warrant, ECG/electrolytes in patients at QT risk, and concentrations/effects of interacting drugs.

Erythromycin is present in human milk; monitor the infant for gastrointestinal effects and consider the infantile-pyloric-stenosis signal.
Use caution in hepatic dysfunction because erythromycin is concentrated and excreted by the liver and can cause hepatotoxicity.
Pediatric use is indication- and dose-specific; infants require particular attention to hypertrophic pyloric stenosis risk.

Overdose can intensify gastrointestinal, hepatic, auditory, and cardiac adverse effects; discontinue the drug and provide supportive care with ECG and interaction assessment.
Macrolide hallmark: 50S/23S-rRNA binding and inhibition of translocation; erythromycin also has prominent GI effects, QT risk, and CYP3A interactions.

Treatment of specified serious systemic fungal infections only when other effective antifungal therapy is unavailable or not tolerated.

Ketoconazole is an oral steroidogenesis inhibitor used in selected patients with Cushing syndrome when surgery is not possible or hypercortisolism persists; liver toxicity and major drug interactions require close monitoring, and this is not an approved indication in the cited U.S. label.

Boxed warning: oral ketoconazole can cause severe/fatal hepatotoxicity and dangerous drug interactions/QT prolongation; use only when other effective antifungal options are unavailable or not tolerated.
Contraindicated in acute or chronic liver disease and with numerous CYP3A substrates whose increased exposure can cause life-threatening toxicity or QT prolongation.
Contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to ketoconazole.
Obtain baseline liver assessment and avoid use when hepatic risk is unacceptable; discontinue promptly for biochemical or clinical evidence of liver injury.
Evaluate adrenal function in patients at risk or with symptoms, especially during stress, prolonged therapy, or high doses.
Elimination is biphasic, with an initial half-life near 2 hours and a terminal half-life near 8 hours in the cited label.
Extensively metabolized hepatically and is a strong CYP3A inhibitor with broad interaction potential.
Metabolites and unchanged drug are eliminated mainly through feces/bile, with a smaller urinary contribution.
Gastric acidity is important for oral dissolution and absorption; acid-suppressing drugs can substantially reduce exposure.
Strong CYP3A inhibition creates extensive contraindicated or dose-limited interactions; review the complete medication list before prescribing.
Proton-pump inhibitors, H2 blockers, antacids, and other gastric-pH-raising agents can impair absorption; administration strategies must follow the label.

Blocks DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, rapidly selects resistance if used alone for active TB, strongly induces drug metabolism, and turns body fluids orange-red.
